If you run an agent on that model you need those bytes, not a close copy. That is the main reason model weights suit BitTorrent better than most of what BitTorrent was built for. They are large, public, never change once published, and a lot of people want the identical files. Search a torrent site for a film and you get a 4K remux, a 1080p encode, a 720p rip, and a few more with different subtitles. Each is a separate torrent with a handful of peers, and most people grab whichever one plays. Nobody does that with a model. Everyone who wants DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 wants the same 48 shards. There is a loose parallel with the web in the 1990s. Many people first got online through AOL, and you found sites through hand-made directories like Yahoo or keyword engines like AltaVista. Google showed up in 1998, ranked pages by the links between them, and became the way most people used the web. Model distribution looks a bit like the pre-Google web today: new open models every week, agents downloading them unattended, and copies spread across servers, mirrors and swarms with nothing tying them together. Those swarms exist whether or not Pirate Face does. To make a torrent, a client cuts the files into equal-sized pieces and hashes each piece. The piece hashes, file names and piece size go into a structure called the info dictionary. The SHA-1 of that structure is the infohash , a 40-character hex string that identifies the torrent. Build a torrent from the same files with the same settings and you get the same infohash, no matter who builds it. Change a single byte and it changes. Popular releases soon get derivatives: quantizations, abliterated versions, and NVFP4, MLX or GGUF conversions. Each of those is its own set of files with its own swarm, and that is correct: a 2-bit GGUF really is a different model. Every Pirate Face magnet includes udp://tracker.pirateface.co:6969/announce . A distributed hash table (DHT) answers the same question without a central server. It is a key-value table spread across many machines: the key is an infohash and the value is a list of peers. BitTorrent's Mainline DHT ( BEP 5 ) is run by millions of ordinary torrent clients. Each node picks a random 160-bit ID, the same length as an infohash, and the distance between two IDs is their XOR. The peer list for a torrent is stored on the nodes whose IDs are closest to its infohash. To find peers, a client asks the closest nodes it already knows. They reply with nodes that are closer still. Each hop roughly halves the distance, so even in a network of millions it takes only a handful of hops. A DHT lookup only finds peers who used the same infohash. For films that produces thousands of tiny peer lists, and you still need an index to pick one. For models, anyone who packages the release the same way computes the same infohash and finds everyone else. In a swarm, downloaders upload as well, so more users means more capacity. What is still missing is a layer on top that says which infohash is the real release, whether its files match the publisher's checksums, how healthy its swarm is, and where each derivative came from.
